lesson_title: The Toll Collector: Energy Conservation and Power
hook_text: The slide is warm at the bottom. That warmth is stolen energy — and physics can tell you exactly how much.
clip_script: A thirty-kilogram child at the top of a three-metre slide is holding 882 joules of height-money. Physics says: if the slide were perfectly slippery, every cent converts to speed, and she arrives at nearly 7,7 metres per second. But measure her at the bottom: only 6. Count her wallet — 540 joules of speed-money. So where are the missing 342 joules? Feel the slide. It's warm. Friction is a toll collector: it charges per metre, keeps the money, and burns it as heat. Gravity, meanwhile, is an honest banker — whatever it charges you to climb, it repays in full on the way down, by any route. That's the entire difference between conservative and non-conservative forces, and one equation reads the receipt: the work of the toll collectors equals the change in kinetic energy plus the change in potential energy. Missing money? Friction took it. Extra money? An engine paid it in. And power? Power is just how FAST the money moves. Run up the stairs instead of walking: same work, same joules — but half the time, double the watts. You, sprinting, are worth about half a kettle.
visual_style: Energy as gold coins: a full purse at the top of a slide, coins trickling into a toll booth along the surface and glowing red as heat, a lighter purse at the bottom; end with two stick figures on stairs and wattage meters racing.
mood: Storybook economics with a detective twist — following stolen joules.
pacing: Set-up of the missing money, warm-slide reveal, brisk banker-versus-toll-collector contrast, playful wattage close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read friction's receipt in any Paper 1 question.
